[10] The RPD found that the Appellants would not face a serious possibility of persecution or a risk to their lives in the IFA location. The Appellants' memorandum makes significant references to the tests under section 96 and 97 but does not actually advance any substantial argument about the Appellants having a nexus to the convention. Having independently reviewed the record, I find that the Appellants do not have a nexus to the Refugee Convention. Their alleged risk is based on being targeted for extortion by a cartel rather than a risk linked to the Convention grounds. There is nothing to suggest that the Appellants' failure to pay the extortion amount to Los Zetas would lead to them being perceived to have an anti-cartel political opinion. The Appellants made no denunciation against the cartel, nor did they express any political opinion that would have a nexus to the convention. The Appellants do advance significant arguments about their risk being personalized, arguing that they were personally targeted and therefore their risk would fall within section 97 of the IRPA. I agree with this argument and note that the RPD also seemed to accept that the Appellants alleged a personalized risk. Therefore, I will assess their risk under section 97.
The Principal Appellant's delay in making a refugee claim detracts from the credibility of the allegations.

[11] The RPD found that the Principal Appellant's delay in advancing a refugee claim diminished the credibility of his allegations. The RPD noted that it asked the Principal Appellant about this delay at the hearing, although it misspoke and asked about a delay of 2 and half months, when in reality the delay was over two years. The RPD noted that the Principal Appellant replied that he believed he would be deported if he made a claim because he is Mexican. The RPD did not accept this explanation. The RPD accepted that the delay in claiming alone was not determinative of the Appellants' claims but found that the delay in making a refugee claim detracted from the credibility of the Appellants' allegations.

[12] The Appellants do not contest this finding.

[13] I agree with the RPD's uncontested finding that the Principal Appellant's delay in making a claim detracts from the credibility of the allegations. I note that when the RPD asked the Principal Appellant why he came to Canada, he testified that he came to seek safety. The RPD asked the Principal Appellant what efforts he made to find out about making a claim and he testified that he just listened to other people and didn't speak English.3 As noted by the RPD, the Principal Appellant made an application to extend his visitor's status, and therefore demonstrated some level of ability to make immigration applications. I agree with the RPD that the Principal Appellant did not provide a reasonable justification for not advancing a claim sooner. I agree that while this delay is not determinative of the Appellants' claim on its own, the delay does detract from the credibility of the Appellants' allegations.
The Appellants' evidence about the events that allegedly occurred after the Principal Appellant left Mexico is inconsistent.

[14] The RPD found that the Principal Appellant's evidence about what happened after he left Mexico was inconsistent. The RPD noted that when it asked the Principal Appellant about what happened in Mexico after he left, he initially testified that the only thing that happened was that the police allegedly visited his home in 2019 but failed to mention the allegation that Los Zetas threatened his tenants in 2018. The RPD noted that the Principal Appellant only mentioned the alleged threatening of his tenants under examination by counsel. The RPD found that this impugned the credibility of the Appellants' allegation that Los Zetas attended their former home looking for them and threatened their tenants in 2018.

[15] The RPD also noted that the Principal Appellant testified that he learned that individuals dressed as police officers attended his family's residence in 2019 through his wife who was informed by a neighbour. However, the RPD noted that the Appellant could not explain why the letter from his neighbour failed to mention this incident. The RPD also highlighted that the Appellants' Basis of Claim narrative indicated that their neighbour was told that there was a warrant for the Principal Appellant by the individuals who presented themselves as police officers, however the letter from this neighbour also failed to mention any such warrant. The RPD concluded that the letter from the Appellants' neighbour would be given no weight due to its failure to mention the alleged visit by people presenting themselves as police officers.

[16] The RPD noted that the Principal Appellant highlighted that he submitted letters from his uncle and father, who allegedly confronted the individuals who presented themselves as police officers. However, the RPD found that these letters were problematic as the letters were inconsistent. The RPD remarked that the letter from the Principal Appellant's father failed to mention what happened when he and the Principal Appellant's uncle confronted these individuals. In contrast, the letter from the Principal Appellant's uncle indicated that he had a gun pointed at him, was assaulted, and was threatened with death. The RPD found that these inconsistencies raised doubts about the credibility of the letters and therefore it gave them little weight. The RPD found that these inconsistencies impugned the credibility of the Appellants' allegation that individuals purporting to be police attended their former residence looking for them in 2019.

[17] The Appellants do not contest these findings in their memorandum.

They argue that this risk would be at the hands of the other cartels operating in Baja California Sur. The Appellants also argue that Los Zetas could track them throughout Mexico through collusion with the police. The Appellants also repeat many of the arguments in their initial Appellant's record, including that their risk is personalized and that the Federal Court has found that there is no IFA from Los Zetas in Mexico.

[30] After independently reviewing the record and considering the Appellant's submissions, I find that the Appellants have a viable IFA in Cabos San Lucas. I find that Los Zetas does not have the means and motivation to locate the Appellants in Cabos San Lucas.

[31] I accept that the Appellants' allegations relate to a personalized risk rather than a generalized risk. However, for the reasons I have set out, I agree with the RPD's determination that the Appellants were not pursued by Los Zetas in 2018 and 2019. I also have credibility concerns with the Appellants' allegations that the Principal Appellant was targeted by Los Zetas given his delay in making a refugee claim. However, even accepting that he was approached by Los Zetas in 2017, I find that they would not have continued motivation to track the Appellants. I find that the Appellants have not credibly established that Los Zetas has made any efforts to locate them after the initial alleged interaction in 2017. I would also note, in the alternative, that if I believed that the cartel attended the Appellants' home twice in two years this does not establish that they would track the Appellants throughout Mexico. There is no indication that the Los Zetas was able to track the Appellants after they left that residence.

[32] The Principal Appellant's evidence is that he was approached by Los Zetas because they wrongly believed he was involved with a rival cartel, however he was able to convince them that this was not the case. The cartel then demanded he make monthly payments to them

[33] Contrary to the Appellants' submissions, the Appellants did not report this to the police or make any public denunciation against the cartel. The reference to the Appellants going to the police and openly challenging the cartel's authority with local merchants13 seems to be misplaced in the Appellants' memorandum and might be an oversight, perhaps from another case or previous memorandum by counsel. In any event, the Appellants' evidence is that they did not go to the police14 and were not involved in any open challenge of the cartel's authority. Instead, the Principal Appellant indicates that he agreed to pay the demand then went into hiding and left Mexico.

[34] I note that reports in the NDP indicate that large debts or personal vendettas can motivate Los Zetas to track individuals outside of their area of control.15 However, I find that the Appellants did not engage in any behaviour that would motivate the cartel to track them across Mexico. Even accepting that Los Zetas sought a monthly quota from the Appellants, I find that this is insufficient to motivate the cartel to track them across Mexico.

[35] Further, I find that the Appellants have not established a political profile that would lead them to be targeted by Los Zetas or cartels generally. Again, while the Appellants' submissions make reference to this, their evidence does not indicate that they were involved in any attempts to challenge the cartels or have a political opinion that would put them at risk. I find that their failure to pay the extortion money as requested by the Los Zetas cartel does not establish either and actual or imputed political opinion.

[36] In considering the objective evidence about Los Zetas, I find that the cartel maps in the NDP indicate that the Los Zetas are not the dominant cartel in Cabo San Lucas or Baja California Sur generally.16 The objective evidence highlights that the Los Zetas cartel has dissolved into smaller groups with their own priorities and alliances following the arrests of several of their leaders.17 While I accept the Appellants' argument that Los Zetas have been involved in acts of brutality and have had links to corrupt law enforcement, I note the evidence generally highlights the decline and splintering in the recent years. As noted in one of the articles provided by the Appellants to the RPD, the leadership of the cartel has been decimated by arrests of various leaders and the group has splintered.18 The objective evidence highlights that the police have dismantled many of these cartel's surveillance networks, although some have been re-established.19

[37] Turning to the Federal Court decision cited by the Appellants, while I accept that the Court found the RAD was unreasonable in concluding that the Appellants had a viable IFA from Los Zetas, I disagree with the Appellants' argument that this decision stands for the proposition that there is no IFA for all individuals fearing Los Zetas in Mexico. I note that in the case referenced by the Appellants, the RPD considered the IFA of Cancun, which the objective evidence indicated was within contested territory with a presence of Los Zetas. I accept the Court's comments that the objective evidence indicates that Los Zetas is a splintered cartel that still has a widespread presence in Mexico and has killed individuals who refuse to work for them. However, this is distinguishable from the Appellants' case as there is no allegation that Los Zetas attempted to recruit the Principal Appellant to work for them. Again, I accept that not withstanding the splintering of the cartel, Los Zetas can track individuals who have a large debt to them or where there is a motivation of personal vendettas. In the Appellants' case, I find that the cartel would have insufficient motivation to track them across Mexico via these splintered networks.

[38] Finally, while the Appellants reference a decision from the RPD,20 they have not provided the decision or the factual background of that case. The decision is not published and without more information I am unable to compare that situation to the Appellants' allegations. I find that the RPD's determination on an individual file, especially without the actual decision or facts, is not persuasive.

REASONS FOR DECISION
OVERVIEW

[1] XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX (Principal Appellant), XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX, and XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX (Associate Appellants) are citizens of Mexico. They appeal a decision of the Refugee Protection Division (RPD) dated October 8, 2020 rejecting their claims. The Appellants allege that they face a serious possibility of persecution and a risk to their lives at the hands of the Los Zetas cartel. The RPD found that the Appellants' allegations were not credible and in the alternative concluded that they had a viable Internal Flight Alternative (IFA) in Merida or Campeche.
[2] For the reasons that follow, the appeal is dismissed.
BACKGROUND

[3] The Principal Appellant alleges that he was approached by a member of the Los Zetas cartel in XXXX 2017. He alleges that he was accused of being involved with a rival cartel, and his assailant checked his identification and went to his home to verify his identity with his wife (the Adult Associate Appellant). The Appellants alleges that he was able to convince his assailant that he was not involved with cartels. He alleges that he was told that he had to pay a monthly ransom demand of $XXXX XXXX XXXX pesos or the Zetas would kill him and harm his family. The Appellant alleges that he was afraid to report the incident to the police as his assailant told him that doing so would lead to him being hurt.

[4] The Appellant alleges that following these threats, he moved into a friend's home and his wife and children moved in with his sister. The Appellant alleges that he received additional threats on the phone, which caused him to fear for his safety. The Appellant alleges he secured a valid passport and travelled to Canada in XXXX 2017. The Appellants allege that they rented out their previous residence and that their tenants were visited and threatened by members of Los Zetas, which caused them to move out of the residence. The Appellants also allege that individuals dressed police officers attended their former residence looking for them in XXXX 2019. The Associate Appellants left Mexico and travelled to Canada in XXXX 2019. The Principal Appellant submitted his basis of claim forms in XXXX 2019 and the Associate Appellants filed theirs in XXXX 2019. The claims were heard jointly by the RPD.
ROLE OF THE REFUGEE APPEAL DIVISION

[5] The Refugee Appeal Division (RAD) reviews decisions of the RPD on a standard of correctness after conducting an independent assessment of the evidence before it. Unless specifically stated below, I have applied a correctness standard.1
ANALYSIS
[6] The Appellants argue that the RPD erred when it concluded that they had a viable IFA and argue.

[7] that they face a serious possibility of persecution and a personalized risk to their lives throughout Mexico. The Appellants argue that Los Zetas operates across Mexico and could locate them in the IFA location. They also argue that the RPD failed to properly consider the objective evidence about the brutality of the cartel. The Appellants also make arguments about their inability to access adequate state protection, although this was not a determinative issue in their claims and the RPD made no findings about state protection.

[8] The RAD wrote to the Appellants and raised the issue of whether they would have a viable IFA in Cabos San Lucas. The Appellants made further arguments in response to this, and these submissions will be considered with their appeal.

[9] I note that the Appellants make no arguments about the RPD's findings about the credibility of their allegations or its analysis of their supporting documents. There also appear to be references in the Appellants' memorandum to facts and names not related to their claims2 which may be an oversight by their counsel. As these arguments are not related to the case before me, they will not be considered.
The Appellants do not have a nexus to the Refugee Convention

[10] The RPD found that the Appellants would not face a serious possibility of persecution or a risk to their lives in the IFA location. The Appellants' memorandum makes significant references to the tests under section 96 and 97 but does not actually advance any substantial argument about the Appellants having a nexus to the convention. Having independently reviewed the record, I find that the Appellants do not have a nexus to the Refugee Convention. Their alleged risk is based on being targeted for extortion by a cartel rather than a risk linked to the Convention grounds. There is nothing to suggest that the Appellants' failure to pay the extortion amount to Los Zetas would lead to them being perceived to have an anti-cartel political opinion. The Appellants made no denunciation against the cartel, nor did they express any political opinion that would have a nexus to the convention. The Appellants do advance significant arguments about their risk being personalized, arguing that they were personally targeted and therefore their risk would fall within section 97 of the IRPA. I agree with this argument and note that the RPD also seemed to accept that the Appellants alleged a personalized risk. Therefore, I will assess their risk under section 97.
The Principal Appellant's delay in making a refugee claim detracts from the credibility of the allegations.

[11] The RPD found that the Principal Appellant's delay in advancing a refugee claim diminished the credibility of his allegations. The RPD noted that it asked the Principal Appellant about this delay at the hearing, although it misspoke and asked about a delay of 2 and half months, when in reality the delay was over two years. The RPD noted that the Principal Appellant replied that he believed he would be deported if he made a claim because he is Mexican. The RPD did not accept this explanation. The RPD accepted that the delay in claiming alone was not determinative of the Appellants' claims but found that the delay in making a refugee claim detracted from the credibility of the Appellants' allegations.
[12] The Appellants do not contest this finding.

[13] I agree with the RPD's uncontested finding that the Principal Appellant's delay in making a claim detracts from the credibility of the allegations. I note that when the RPD asked the Principal Appellant why he came to Canada, he testified that he came to seek safety. The RPD asked the Principal Appellant what efforts he made to find out about making a claim and he testified that he just listened to other people and didn't speak English.3 As noted by the RPD, the Principal Appellant made an application to extend his visitor's status, and therefore demonstrated some level of ability to make immigration applications. I agree with the RPD that the Principal Appellant did not provide a reasonable justification for not advancing a claim sooner. I agree that while this delay is not determinative of the Appellants' claim on its own, the delay does detract from the credibility of the Appellants' allegations.
The Appellants' evidence about the events that allegedly occurred after the Principal Appellant left Mexico is inconsistent.

[14] The RPD found that the Principal Appellant's evidence about what happened after he left Mexico was inconsistent. The RPD noted that when it asked the Principal Appellant about what happened in Mexico after he left, he initially testified that the only thing that happened was that the police allegedly visited his home in 2019 but failed to mention the allegation that Los Zetas threatened his tenants in 2018. The RPD noted that the Principal Appellant only mentioned the alleged threatening of his tenants under examination by counsel. The RPD found that this impugned the credibility of the Appellants' allegation that Los Zetas attended their former home looking for them and threatened their tenants in 2018.

[15] The RPD also noted that the Principal Appellant testified that he learned that individuals dressed as police officers attended his family's residence in 2019 through his wife who was informed by a neighbour. However, the RPD noted that the Appellant could not explain why the letter from his neighbour failed to mention this incident. The RPD also highlighted that the Appellants' Basis of Claim narrative indicated that their neighbour was told that there was a warrant for the Principal Appellant by the individuals who presented themselves as police officers, however the letter from this neighbour also failed to mention any such warrant. The RPD concluded that the letter from the Appellants' neighbour would be given no weight due to its failure to mention the alleged visit by people presenting themselves as police officers.

[16] The RPD noted that the Principal Appellant highlighted that he submitted letters from his uncle and father, who allegedly confronted the individuals who presented themselves as police officers. However, the RPD found that these letters were problematic as the letters were inconsistent. The RPD remarked that the letter from the Principal Appellant's father failed to mention what happened when he and the Principal Appellant's uncle confronted these individuals. In contrast, the letter from the Principal Appellant's uncle indicated that he had a gun pointed at him, was assaulted, and was threatened with death. The RPD found that these inconsistencies raised doubts about the credibility of the letters and therefore it gave them little weight. The RPD found that these inconsistencies impugned the credibility of the Appellants' allegation that individuals purporting to be police attended their former residence looking for them in 2019.
[17] The Appellants do not contest these findings in their memorandum.

[18] Having independently reviewed the record, I agree with the RPD's uncontested findings about the credibility of the Appellants' allegations that Los Zetas continued to look for them after the Principal Appellant left Mexico in 2017. I agree with the RPD's finding that the Principal Appellant's failure to mention the alleged threats against their tenants in 2018 impugns the credibility of this allegation. The Principal Appellant was clearly asked if anything happened after he left Mexico and only mentioned the alleged visit of individuals who presented themselves as police officers to his former home in 2019. The RPD then specifically asked the Appellant if anything else happened between 2017 and 2019 and the Principal Appellant responded that there was nothing else.4 The Principal Appellant only mentioned the alleged threatening of the tenants in 2018 when counsel explicitly asked him about his property.5 I agree with the RPD that the Principal Appellant's failure to spontaneously provide this information when he was asked about whether anything happened in Mexico after he left in 2017 detracts from the credibility of the allegation that his tenants were threatened by Los Zetas.

[19] I also agree with the uncontested finding that the Appellant's allegation that individuals purporting to be police officers attended his residence in 2019 is not credible. As noted by the RPD, the letters provided by the Principals Appellant's uncle and father are inconsistent. The letter from the Appellant's father fails to mention the alleged assault against the Principal Appellant's uncle. I agree that this is not a minor detail. I find that the failure of the Principal Appellant's father to mention that the Principal Appellant's uncle was assaulted with a gun and threatened with death detracts from the credibility of the allegation. I agree with the RPD and give the letters from the Appellant's father and uncle little weight.

[20] I also agree that the failure of the Appellants' neighbour to mention that individuals presented themselves as police officers and claimed to have a warrant for the Principal Appellant in his letter detracts from the credibility of this allegation. I agree that given that this neighbour allegedly advised the Adult Associate Appellant that individuals claiming to be police officers were looking for the Appellants it is reasonable to expect that he would mention this in his letter. The letter from the Appellants' neighbour6 makes no mention of Los Zetas or police officers attending the Appellants' residence. Therefore, I agree with the RPD and give this letter no weight.
The Principal Appellant's response to why he feared Los Zetas was not inconsistent and does not detract from the credibility of his allegations.

[21] The RPD found that the Principal Appellant's testimony about why he feared Los Zetas was inconsistent with his other evidence. Specifically, the RPD noted that when it asked the Principal Appellant why he feared the cartel, he testified that it was because he failed to pay the extortion money they demanded. The RPD noted that the Appellants' narrative indicated that the cartel targeted the Principal Appellant because it believed that he was working for a rival cartel. The RPD found that the Principal Appellant's failure to mention this detracted from the credibility of his allegation.

[22] While the Appellants make no arguments about this finding, I have independently reviewed the record and I find that the RPD erred in determining that the Principal Appellant's testimony was inconsistent with his other evidence. While the Principal Appellant did respond that he feared Los Zetas because he had not paid the extortion money, he also testified that he was targeted because the cartel mistakenly believed he was working for a rival cartel. A careful review of the audio of the RPD hearing supports the Principal Appellant's explanation that he believed the initial question about why he was afraid was related to the extortion demands. Put simply, the Principal Appellant's testimony that he feared the cartel because he did not pay them the money they demanded was a reasonable response, as the RPD did not ask why the Principal Appellant was initially targeted. When the Principal Appellant was asked directly by his counsel why Los Zetas approached him, he replied that they thought he worked for another cartel.7 Therefore, I find that the Principal Appellant's testimony about this issue is consistent with his other evidence
Summary on credibility findings.

[23] For the reasons I have outlined, there is a concern with the credibility of the Appellants' allegations. I find that the Appellants' allegations that the Los Zetas continued to look for them following the Principal Appellant's departure from Mexico in 2017 are not credible. I find that even if I accept that the Principal Appellant was approached by the Los Zetas in 2017 and demand he pay them extortion money, the Appellants have a viable IFA in Cabos San Lucas.
The Appellants have a viable IFA in Cabos San Lucas

[24] The test for assessing an IFA is two-pronged and is set out in the Federal Court of Appeal's decision in Rasaratnam:8
(1) The Board must be satisfied on a balance of probabilities that there is no serious possibility of the claimant being persecuted in the part of the country to which it finds an IFA exists and/or the claimant would not be personally subject to a risk to life or risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment or danger, believed on substantial grounds to exist, of torture in the IFA.
(2) Moreover, the conditions in the part of the country considered to be an IFA must be such that it would not be unreasonable in all the circumstances, including those particular to the claim, for the claimant to seek refuge there.

[25] Both prongs must be satisfied to find that the Appellant has an IFA. Once the issue of IFA has been raised and the potential IFAs have been identified, the burden of proof rests with the Appellant to show that they do not have an IFA. An IFA must be a realistic and attainable option.9
First prong: Do the agents of harm have the means and motivation to locate the Appellants in Cabo San Lucas?

[26] The RPD found that the Los Zetas cartel did not have the means or motivation to locate the Appellants in Merida or Campeche. The RPD acknowledged that the cartel map in the record indicated that there was some level of Zetas activity in the region. However, the RPD found that the Los Zetas had suffered a decline in its influence and had splintered into fragmented splinter groups. The RPD also concluded that the Zetas activity in the Yucatan region was concentrated in cities outside of Merida and Campeche.

[27] The RPD also noted that it had concerns with the credibility of the Appellants' allegations that Los Zetas had pursued them in 2018 and 2019 and found on a balance of probabilities that Los Zetas had not been pursuing the Appellants. The RPD went on to find that even if it were to accept that the cartel had in fact tried to locate the Appellants on those occasions, there was no indication that Los Zetas had made any efforts to locate the Appellants in over a year. The RPD found that the Appellants' failure to pay the extortion demands was insufficient for a Zetas faction to expend the effort and cost to pursue them.

[28] The Appellants argue that the risk they face is personalized due to their failure to comply with specific extortion demands of the Zetas and the threats of revenge they received. The Appellants argue that the RPD failed to adequately consider the malicious and vindictive motivations of the Los Zetas Cartel. They also argue that they "openly defied the purported authority of the Los Zetas Cartel, involving the police and challenging their authority among the general merchant public."10 The Appellants argue that Los Zetas has broad influence and powers which would allow the cartel to locate them anywhere in Mexico. The Appellants also cite a decision of the Federal Court,11 which they argue establishes that there is no viable IFA from Los Zetas.

[29] The Appellants filed additional submissions in response to the RAD raising the new issue of an IFA in Cabo San Lucas. The Appellants concede that Los Zetas does not have a significant presence in Cabo San Lucas but argue that this does not mitigate their forward-looking risk. The Appellants' counsel cites a RPD decision (TB8-32937) where they argue the RPD agreed with counsel's argument that there was no IFA from Los Zetas in Mexico.12 The Appellants also argue that they face a serious possibility of persecution in the new IFA location due to their political opinion of being in opposition to cartels. They argue that this risk would be at the hands of the other cartels operating in Baja California Sur. The Appellants also argue that Los Zetas could track them throughout Mexico through collusion with the police. The Appellants also repeat many of the arguments in their initial Appellant's record, including that their risk is personalized and that the Federal Court has found that there is no IFA from Los Zetas in Mexico.

[30] After independently reviewing the record and considering the Appellant's submissions, I find that the Appellants have a viable IFA in Cabos San Lucas. I find that Los Zetas does not have the means and motivation to locate the Appellants in Cabos San Lucas.

[31] I accept that the Appellants' allegations relate to a personalized risk rather than a generalized risk. However, for the reasons I have set out, I agree with the RPD's determination that the Appellants were not pursued by Los Zetas in 2018 and 2019. I also have credibility concerns with the Appellants' allegations that the Principal Appellant was targeted by Los Zetas given his delay in making a refugee claim. However, even accepting that he was approached by Los Zetas in 2017, I find that they would not have continued motivation to track the Appellants. I find that the Appellants have not credibly established that Los Zetas has made any efforts to locate them after the initial alleged interaction in 2017. I would also note, in the alternative, that if I believed that the cartel attended the Appellants' home twice in two years this does not establish that they would track the Appellants throughout Mexico. There is no indication that the Los Zetas was able to track the Appellants after they left that residence.

[32] The Principal Appellant's evidence is that he was approached by Los Zetas because they wrongly believed he was involved with a rival cartel, however he was able to convince them that this was not the case. The cartel then demanded he make monthly payments to them

[33] Contrary to the Appellants' submissions, the Appellants did not report this to the police or make any public denunciation against the cartel. The reference to the Appellants going to the police and openly challenging the cartel's authority with local merchants13 seems to be misplaced in the Appellants' memorandum and might be an oversight, perhaps from another case or previous memorandum by counsel. In any event, the Appellants' evidence is that they did not go to the police14 and were not involved in any open challenge of the cartel's authority. Instead, the Principal Appellant indicates that he agreed to pay the demand then went into hiding and left Mexico.

[34] I note that reports in the NDP indicate that large debts or personal vendettas can motivate Los Zetas to track individuals outside of their area of control.15 However, I find that the Appellants did not engage in any behaviour that would motivate the cartel to track them across Mexico. Even accepting that Los Zetas sought a monthly quota from the Appellants, I find that this is insufficient to motivate the cartel to track them across Mexico.

[35] Further, I find that the Appellants have not established a political profile that would lead them to be targeted by Los Zetas or cartels generally. Again, while the Appellants' submissions make reference to this, their evidence does not indicate that they were involved in any attempts to challenge the cartels or have a political opinion that would put them at risk. I find that their failure to pay the extortion money as requested by the Los Zetas cartel does not establish either and actual or imputed political opinion.

[36] In considering the objective evidence about Los Zetas, I find that the cartel maps in the NDP indicate that the Los Zetas are not the dominant cartel in Cabo San Lucas or Baja California Sur generally.16 The objective evidence highlights that the Los Zetas cartel has dissolved into smaller groups with their own priorities and alliances following the arrests of several of their leaders.17 While I accept the Appellants' argument that Los Zetas have been involved in acts of brutality and have had links to corrupt law enforcement, I note the evidence generally highlights the decline and splintering in the recent years. As noted in one of the articles provided by the Appellants to the RPD, the leadership of the cartel has been decimated by arrests of various leaders and the group has splintered.18 The objective evidence highlights that the police have dismantled many of these cartel's surveillance networks, although some have been re-established.19

[37] Turning to the Federal Court decision cited by the Appellants, while I accept that the Court found the RAD was unreasonable in concluding that the Appellants had a viable IFA from Los Zetas, I disagree with the Appellants' argument that this decision stands for the proposition that there is no IFA for all individuals fearing Los Zetas in Mexico. I note that in the case referenced by the Appellants, the RPD considered the IFA of Cancun, which the objective evidence indicated was within contested territory with a presence of Los Zetas. I accept the Court's comments that the objective evidence indicates that Los Zetas is a splintered cartel that still has a widespread presence in Mexico and has killed individuals who refuse to work for them. However, this is distinguishable from the Appellants' case as there is no allegation that Los Zetas attempted to recruit the Principal Appellant to work for them. Again, I accept that not withstanding the splintering of the cartel, Los Zetas can track individuals who have a large debt to them or where there is a motivation of personal vendettas. In the Appellants' case, I find that the cartel would have insufficient motivation to track them across Mexico via these splintered networks.

[38] Finally, while the Appellants reference a decision from the RPD,20 they have not provided the decision or the factual background of that case. The decision is not published and without more information I am unable to compare that situation to the Appellants' allegations. I find that the RPD's determination on an individual file, especially without the actual decision or facts, is not persuasive.

[39] For these reasons I find that the Appellants do not face a risk to their lives or cruel or unusual treatment or punishment in Cabo San Lucas.
Second prong: Is it unreasonable for the Appellants to relocate to Cabo San Lucas?

[40] The RPD found that the Appellants could relocate to Merida or Campeche and noted that aside from their alleged fear of Los Zetas, the Appellants did not make any arguments about why they could not relocate to the proposed IFAs.

[41] The Appellants do not offer any arguments about why they could not relocate within Mexico aside from their arguments that they fear Los Zetas and cartels generally. When the RAD raised the IFA in Cabo San Lucas the Appellants did not advance any reasons, aside from these concerns with cartels, that they could not relocate.

[42] I find that the Appellants could reasonably relocate to Cabo San Lucas. For the reasons I have set out, I find that the Appellants have not established that they would face a forward-looking risk of being targeted by cartels. While I acknowledge that cartel violence is an issue throughout Mexico, I find that this generalized risk is insufficient to make relocation to Cabo San Lucas unreasonable. Both Adult Appellants have employment history and experience with international relocation which could assist them in establishing their family in Cabo San Lucas. There is no indication of any linguistic or logistical barrier to the Appellants moving to Cabo San Lucas. Therefore, I find that the Appellants have not established that relocating to Cabo San Lucas is unreasonable.
State Protection
[43] As I find that the Appellants have a viable IFA, I will not go on to consider their arguments about state protection.
CONCLUSION

[44] I dismiss the appeal and confirm the decision of the RPD that the Appellants are neither Convention refugees nor persons in need of protection.
(signed)
J. Lourenço
